# The Easy Way to Stop

> "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
>
> — 1 John 1:9

This is the chapter with the instructions in it. Follow them and you'll find stopping somewhere between easy and enjoyable. There are only two:

1. **Decide that you will never do it again.**
2. **Don't mope about it. Rejoice.**

The Bible has older names for both. The first is *repentance*. The word doesn't mean feeling dreadful. It means a change of mind: you turn round and walk the other way. The second is *receiving grace*. You're forgiven, so you act like a forgiven man.

Decide and rejoice, or repent and receive. That's the whole method.

"Then why nineteen chapters? Why didn't you say so on page one?"

Because you've done the first half before. You decided, with tears, more times than you can count. Then you moped, the moping turned to craving, and one grey evening you un-decided. The decision was never the hard part. Your decisions didn't stick because you still believed you were giving something up. That belief is the Big Monster, and it had to be dismantled lie by lie before these two lines could do their work. Once you know how the trap is built, walking out of it is simple.

## My last time {-}

I spent years on the other method. I made vows at retreats and on New Year's Day, and on a good many mornings when I couldn't look at myself. Each time I failed I consoled myself with the same thought: next time will be easier.

Then one day a different thought arrived, and it frightened me properly. *What if there is no "next time" that works? What if I simply do this for the rest of my life?* I pictured myself at fifty, at seventy, still locking the door. For once I stopped vowing and started thinking.

The next time the urge came, I didn't obey it on autopilot. I watched. I asked what I was actually getting, and the honest answer was what I'd half known for years: I wasn't enjoying it. I hadn't for a long time. There were a few seconds of relief and then the familiar flatness.

Then I started watching other men. I'd always assumed the ones who didn't do it were either liars or a bit bloodless. But the men I knew who were plainly free of it weren't bloodless at all. They seemed steadier than me and more at ease, with more life in them, not less. And when I got talking to men who'd quit, I expected to find them hanging on by their fingernails. One or two said the thought still crossed their mind now and then and wasn't worth worrying about. Most of them laughed. "Miss it? You're joking."

Those conversations knocked down the last thing I believed about myself, which was that I had some defect other men didn't. Every one of them had been through the same private misery. The fault was in the trap and never in me.

So I reasoned it through. Plenty of men are living happily without this. I didn't need it before I started. I don't enjoy it now. I do not want to be its servant at seventy. And I said to myself, out loud:

"Like it or not, that was the last time."

I knew as I said it that it was true. I expected the worst: months of climbing the walls and a lifetime of twinges. What I got was relief on the first day, and it has never left.

For a long while I couldn't explain why that attempt went so smoothly. The answer is that the terrible cravings I'd braced for don't exist. Doubt creates them. A man suffers only when he wants it and thinks he can't have it. Even in the trap you go whole days without it when you're busy or travelling, and you barely notice. The misery comes from the dithering, the "maybe just tonight", the door left ajar.

So the key is to make it certain and final. Don't hope you've stopped. Know it. But how can a man be certain at the very start? That is what the rest of the book is for.

## Five things to be clear on {-}

Get these straight before you decide.

1. **You can do it.** You're no different from the men who are already out. And nobody can make you do it except you. The woman in your memory certainly can't. She has no idea she's being used.
2. **There is nothing to give up.** You gain on every side: energy, time, a clean conscience, your own respect. You'll enjoy the good days more and get through the bad ones better.
3. **"Just once" doesn't exist.** It's a chain, and each link pulls the next. Sighing over the odd occasion only punishes you for nothing.
4. **Call it what it is.** It isn't a harmless bit of "boys will be boys". It is a trap, and for the Christian a sin, that tightens every year and won't go away because you look the other way. There will never be an easier day to walk out than today.
5. **You are not the habit.** Ask any man in the trap whether he'd take the chance to go back to the day before he started, and he'd grab it. That chance is in front of you now. Don't call it "giving up".

## You're free the moment you decide {-}

When you make that decision, you're already a man who doesn't do it. You don't become one after ninety days or after the Little Monster dies. You become one in that moment. A recovery writer put the new identity in a single line: "Begin to say, I am a man (or woman) who does not use pornography, masturbate, or lust."

So don't sit about waiting for the itch to fade before you allow yourself to be happy. Get out and live straight away.

This is where the Christian has an enormous advantage, if he'll take it. Look at the verse at the head of the chapter. Confess, and He is *faithful* to forgive. It doesn't say He might, or that He will once you've proved yourself with a decent streak. And then: "There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus" (Romans 8:1). The word is *now*, on day one, with the Little Monster still grumbling.

One man, who now teaches other men about this, spent years repenting and falling until he saw what was wrong with his repentance. It was all about him: how bad he was, how hard he'd try. "The foundation of my repentance was me", he says. Then he turned it round, and this is the sentence to carry out of this chapter: "Our motive for repentance is the fact that God is good. Not the fact that you are bad."

A pastor draws the same line between two kinds of sorrow. Worldly sorrow is sorry it got caught, and it defends itself and plays the thing down. Godly sorrow is sad to have grieved someone who loves you. Under that first man's story a listener wrote what the difference had done for him: "'Breaking God's heart' just changed my whole entire mindset." The first kind of sorrow leaves a man staring at himself, and the second gets him looking up.

Remember from Chapter 1 that guilt loads the gun. The man who decides and then spends three weeks feeling filthy is moping in religious clothes, and it ends in the same place. Grace is what makes instruction two possible. You rejoice because the past really is dealt with. A man of forty-three, who had fasted and read his Bible over it for years, summed up his freedom in three words and capital letters: "JESUS DID IT!" That is what rejoicing sounds like, and you can start on the first day.

If you're not a believer, the same advice holds: drop the self-hatred. It never helped you once. Decide, and be glad.

## The thread pays off {-}

From the Introduction on, this book has said that **a man who can't control his lust can't be trusted.** Here is the other half.

You probably thought self-control meant what you'd been doing for years: gripping the rail with white knuckles, with a strong man holding down a strong desire. That's a wrestling match, and you know who usually won.

Real self-control is quieter. It belongs to a man whose mind is no longer divided. He isn't holding anything down, because there's nothing pushing up. Paul lists self-control among the fruit of the Spirit, and fruit grows on a healthy tree without the tree straining. The old preacher Thomas Chalmers explained how a desire actually leaves a heart: "the only way to dispossess it of an old affection is by the expulsive power of a new one." Freedom is a new affection, and so is a clean conscience. Christ is the greatest one there is.

And here is the payoff. The moment you decide and mean it, you have given your word and you're going to keep it. For the first time in years you'll be a man who can believe his own promises. Trust starts there, and your wife, your friends and your work will feel it in time.

## If you feel gloomy {-}

By now, if you've read with an open mind, you should be like a dog pulling at the lead. If what you feel is doom and gloom, it will be for one of three reasons.

1. **Something hasn't clicked.** Go back over the five points and ask of each one, "Do I actually believe this?" Where you doubt, re-read the chapter that covers it.
2. **You're afraid of failing.** Don't be. Keep reading. This whole business is a confidence trick. Clever men get conned all the time. It takes a fool to go on being conned after he's been shown how the trick is done. You've seen it.
3. **You agree with all of it and feel miserable anyway.** Then look up. Something marvellous is going on. You're about to walk out of a prison. Start as you mean to go on: "Isn't it marvellous? I'm free!"

The chapters that follow are there to keep you in that frame of mind through the first weeks. After that you won't need to hold the thought. It'll be how you think, and the only puzzle left will be why you didn't see it years ago.

## Two warnings {-}

**First: don't make your final decision until you finish the book.** I know. You're ready now. But the last step is in Chapter 27. It's a prayer, and there's a little more to put in place before you pray it. Until then, carry on as normal, as Chapter 1 told you.

**Second: don't misread "the first weeks".** The next chapter says the Little Monster takes a few weeks to starve, and that can mislead you in two ways. You may quietly assume you're in for a few weeks of suffering. You aren't. Or you may think, "I just have to hold out for three weeks and then I'll be fine." That's the willpower trap again. Nothing magic happens on day twenty-one. A man who mopes for three weeks will be moping in the fourth, and by then he'll be desperate. But if you start by saying, "I'm never doing that again, and isn't it marvellous?", then by the time those weeks are up the temptation will have gone without your noticing.

You can't order yourself to feel glad about losing something you still think is valuable. Nobody can. That is why this book has spent nineteen chapters showing you that the thing is worthless. You aren't losing anything. Once you know that, the gladness comes by itself.
